title: Relative clauses: defining, non-defining and comment clauses
summary: Use relative clauses to identify which person or thing you mean, to add extra information about something already identified, and to comment on a whole idea.
author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)

blocks.text: A relative clause gives information about a noun. It starts with a relative word (**who**, **which**, **that**, **whose**, **where**, **when**, **why**), or sometimes with no relative word at all.
There are three jobs a relative clause can do, and the job decides the grammar:

items: **Defining**: it tells us *which* one. Without it, the sentence is incomplete or means something else.
**Non-defining**: the noun is already clear; the clause adds extra information. It sits between commas.
**Comment**: a clause with **which** that comments on the whole previous idea, not on one noun.

items.en: Students **who revise little and often** usually remember more.
items.note: Defining: which students? The ones who revise little and often.

items.en: My tutor, **who has taught here for twenty years**, still marks every essay by hand.
items.note: Non-defining: I have one tutor; the clause adds a fact about her.

items.en: The exam was moved to a Saturday, **which annoyed almost everyone**.
items.note: Comment: *which* refers to the whole event of moving the exam.

blocks.text: In a **defining** clause you can leave out the relative word when it is the **object** of the clause: *the course (that) she recommended*. You cannot leave it out when it is the **subject**: *the course that changed my mind*, not ~~the course changed my mind~~.

items.en: The textbook (that) **we were given** is already out of date.
items.note: *that* = object of *were given*, so it can be omitted.

items.en: The textbook **that explains** this best is the old one.
items.note: *that* = subject of *explains*, so it must stay.

items.en: She is the researcher **whose study** changed how we teach reading.
items.note: *whose* + noun shows possession, for people and things.

sections.title: Defining or non-defining? The comma test

blocks.text: Commas are not decoration here: they change the meaning. Ask yourself: **if I remove the clause, do I still know exactly who or what I mean?** If yes, it is non-defining and needs commas. If no, it is defining and takes no commas.

items.en: The students **who had attended every seminar** passed easily.
items.note: Only some students attended every seminar, and those ones passed.

items.en: The students, **who had attended every seminar**, passed easily.
items.note: All the students attended every seminar, and all of them passed.

blocks.text: Proper nouns and nouns that are already unique (*my mother*, *Oxford*, *the head of the department*) almost always take non-defining clauses, because they are already identified.
In speech, a non-defining clause is said as a separate chunk, with a small pause before and after it. Reading your sentence aloud is a fast way to decide whether you need commas.
A non-defining clause starting with **which** can refer back to the **whole previous clause**. This is a very common way to add your opinion or a consequence at the end of a sentence.

items.en: Many universities now record their lectures, **which means** students can review difficult points at their own pace.
He failed his first-year exams, **which was a shock** to everyone who knew him.
The school abolished homework for younger pupils, **which I think was** a sensible decision.

blocks.text: Only **which** works here. *What* and *that* cannot introduce a comment clause.

items.en: ~~The library closes at six, what is inconvenient for part-time students.~~
The library closes at six, **which** is inconvenient for part-time students.

blocks.text: Use **where** after nouns of place, including abstract places like *situation*, *case*, *stage* and *point*.

items.en: This is the lab **where** the first experiments took place.
We reached a point **where** nobody wanted to compromise.
There was a time **when** a degree almost guaranteed a good job.
The reason **(why)** so many students drop out is often financial.

blocks.text: Use *where* only if the clause is complete without a preposition: *the town **where** I studied* or *the town **which** I studied **in***, but not ~~the town where I studied in~~.
When the relative word is the object of a preposition, English gives you two options. They differ in **register**.
After a preposition, use **which** for things and **whom** for people. *That* and *who* cannot follow a preposition.
In academic essays, *in which*, *by which* and *to whom* sound precise and controlled. In conversation they can sound stiff, so end with the preposition instead.
In non-defining clauses you can begin with a quantifier or number followed by **of which** (things) or **of whom** (people). This lets you add a statistic or a detail without starting a new sentence.

items.en: The survey questioned 2,000 graduates, **most of whom** were working in their field.
The course has six modules, **two of which** are assessed by exam.
She published three papers, **none of which** received much attention at the time.
~~My brother, that studies law, lives in Kazan.~~
items.note: No *that* in non-defining clauses. → *My brother, **who** studies law, …*

items.en: ~~The book which I bought it is excellent.~~
items.note: The relative word replaces the object; do not repeat it. → *The book (which) I bought is excellent.*

items.en: ~~Students which plagiarise are expelled.~~
~~He passed every exam what surprised his parents.~~
items.note: Comment clauses need a comma and *which*. → *…every exam, **which** surprised his parents.*

items.en: ~~The university where I applied to rejected me.~~
items.note: Drop either *where* or the preposition. → *The university **(that)** I applied **to** …*

blocks.text: For Russian speakers: *который* covers both *who* and *which*, and Russian puts a comma before every relative clause. In English the comma signals non-defining meaning, so leave it out of defining clauses.

items: Defining clauses identify; no commas; *that* is possible; the object pronoun can be omitted.
Non-defining clauses add information; commas; never *that*; never omitted.
Comment clauses: *, which …* refers to the whole previous idea.
Formal style moves the preposition forward: *in which*, *to whom*.
*most of whom*, *some of which* add details inside a non-defining clause.
